content: Ovulation has been observed to occur as early as 8 to 13 days following the conclusion of a pregnancy. Consequently, the probability of ovulation occurring within 7 days after an abortion is low. A recent systematic review determined that the average time to first ovulation among postpartum non-lactating women is between 45 and 94 days after delivery. In one study, the earliest ovulation was reported at 25 days postpartum. Among women who are within six months postpartum, are exclusively or nearly exclusively breastfeeding, and are amenorrheic, the risk of pregnancy is less than 2%. Although pregnancy tests are commonly performed before initiating contraception, the accuracy of qualitative urine pregnancy tests depends on factors such as the timing of the test relative to missed menses, recent sexual activity, or a recent pregnancy. The sensitivity of a pregnancy test is defined as the concentration of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) at which 95% of tests yield a positive result. Most qualitative pregnancy tests approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) report a sensitivity of 20–25 mIU/mL in urine. However, pregnancy detection rates can vary significantly due to differences in test sensitivity and the timing of testing relative to missed menses. Some studies indicate that an additional 11 days beyond the expected day of menses may be required to detect 100% of pregnancies using qualitative tests. Additionally, pregnancy tests cannot detect pregnancies resulting from very recent sexual intercourse. Qualitative tests may also yield positive results for several weeks after pregnancy termination, as hCG can remain detectable for weeks following delivery or abortion (spontaneous or induced). For contraceptive methods other than intrauterine devices (IUDs), the benefits of initiating contraception generally outweigh any risks, even in cases where the healthcare provider is uncertain about the patient’s pregnancy status. Therefore, healthcare providers may consider starting non-IUD contraceptive methods at any time, with a follow-up pregnancy test in 2–4 weeks. The risks of delaying contraception should be weighed against the risks of initiating contraception in a woman who might already be pregnant. Most studies have shown no increased risk of adverse outcomes, including congenital anomalies or neonatal or infant death, among infants exposed in utero to combined oral contraceptives (COCs). Similarly, studies have shown no increased risk of neonatal or infant death or developmental abnormalities among infants exposed in utero to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA). In contrast, for women who wish to begin using an IUD (either copper or levonorgestrel-releasing), and where the healthcare provider is uncertain about pregnancy status, an alternative contraceptive method should be provided until pregnancy can be reasonably excluded, at which point the IUD can be inserted. Pregnancies in women with IUDs are associated with higher risks of complications, such as spontaneous abortion, septic abortion, preterm delivery, and chorioamnionitis. A systematic review identified four analyses from three diagnostic accuracy studies evaluating the performance of a pregnancy checklist compared with a concurrent urine pregnancy test. The sensitivity of the checklist to diagnose or exclude pregnancy ranged from 55% to 100%, while specificity ranged from 39% to 89%. The negative predictive value was consistently high (99%–100%), indicating that the checklist reliably ruled out pregnancy in non-pregnant women. One study assessed the added value of pregnancy signs and symptoms and found that these criteria did not significantly improve the checklist’s performance, although the sample size of women with such signs and symptoms was small. Three types of IUDs are available in the United States: the copper IUD (Cu-IUD) and two levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs) containing either 13.5 mg or 52 mg of levonorgestrel. Fewer than 1 in 100 women become pregnant during the first year of typical IUD use. IUDs are long-acting, reversible contraceptives suitable for women of all ages, including adolescents, and for both parous and nulliparous women. However, IUDs do not protect against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs); consistent and correct use of male latex condoms is recommended to reduce the risk of STDs, including HIV. The Cu-IUD can be inserted at any time if it is reasonably certain that the woman is not pregnant. It can also be inserted within five days of unprotected sexual intercourse as emergency contraception. If ovulation timing can be estimated, the Cu-IUD may be inserted more than five days after intercourse, provided insertion does not occur more than five days after ovulation. No additional contraceptive protection is needed after Cu-IUD insertion. For postpartum women, including those who have undergone cesarean delivery, the Cu-IUD can be inserted at any time, including immediately postpartum, if it is reasonably certain that the woman is not pregnant. However, the Cu-IUD should not be inserted in women with puerperal sepsis. Similarly, for post-abortion women (spontaneous or induced), the Cu-IUD can be inserted within the first seven days, including immediately post-abortion, provided there is no septic abortion. No additional contraceptive protection is needed after Cu-IUD insertion. When switching from another contraceptive method, the Cu-IUD can be inserted immediately if it is reasonably certain that the woman is not pregnant. Waiting for the next menstrual period is unnecessary, and no additional contraceptive protection is required. In cases where the healthcare provider cannot reasonably exclude pregnancy, an alternative contraceptive method should be provided until pregnancy can be ruled out, at which point the Cu-IUD can be inserted. A systematic review of eight studies suggested that the timing of Cu-IUD insertion relative to the menstrual cycle in non-postpartum women had minimal impact on long-term outcomes (e.g., continuation, removal, expulsion, or pregnancy rates) or short-term outcomes (e.g., pain).
